tool.name: PostgreSQL
tool.tagline: Advanced open-source relational database with rich types and extensions
tool.description: PostgreSQL is a powerful open-source relational database known for correctness, standards compliance and extensibility. Beyond standard SQL it offers jsonb, arrays, ranges, full-text search, many index types and an extension ecosystem (PostGIS, pgvector), and it is the default database for many web back ends. This curriculum covers using it day to day through to operating, tuning and replicating it.

glossary.def: A short psql command that starts with a backslash, such as \dt (list tables). psql handles it itself instead of sending it to the server as SQL.
PostgreSQL's word for a user or a group of users. A role that may log in acts as a user; one that can't is used as a group that other roles join.
In PostgreSQL, a role that skips every permission check and can do anything, such as the postgres role a fresh installation creates. Apps should never connect as one.
A database server rented from a provider such as Amazon RDS, which runs it, backs it up and upgrades it for you; you only connect to it.
The built-in tables in which PostgreSQL keeps its own list of databases, tables, columns, roles and everything else.
In PostgreSQL, one running server together with all the data it manages: several databases plus the roles they share. Not a group of computers.
In PostgreSQL, a named folder inside a database that holds tables, views and functions, such as public or billing. (More generally, the design of a database's tables.)
A PostgreSQL setting listing the schemas to look in, in order, when a query names a table without saying which schema it is in.
In PostgreSQL, one client connection from the moment it logs in until it disconnects. Settings changed with SET last only for the session.
All the details needed to reach a database written as one line, like a web address: postgresql://user:password@host:5432/dbname.
PostgreSQL's file of rules saying who may connect from where, and how they must prove who they are. Rules are read top to bottom; the first match wins.
PostgreSQL's 'timestamp with time zone' type: it stores one exact moment (kept in UTC) and shows it in the time zone of whoever reads it.
In PostgreSQL, a counter stored in the database that hands out the next number each time it's asked; identity and serial columns use one.
PostgreSQL's older shorthand for an auto-numbered column (serial, bigserial). It sets up a sequence plus a default; identity columns are the modern replacement.
A temporary table you load raw data into first, often with all-text columns, so you can clean and check it with SQL before copying it into the real table.
In a database, a right a role holds on something, such as SELECT on a table or CONNECT on a database. Given with GRANT, taken away with REVOKE.
In PostgreSQL, the 8 kB block that table and index data is stored and read in. Reading one row means reading the whole page it sits on.
An add-on that ships with PostgreSQL and writes the query plan of every statement slower than a limit you set into the server's log.
In PostgreSQL, a named data type made from an existing one plus rules, such as an email type that is text with a CHECK; reusable across tables.
PostgreSQL's built-in language for writing functions that run in the database, adding variables, IF, loops and error handling to SQL.
In PostgreSQL, a routine created with CREATE PROCEDURE and run with CALL. Unlike a function it returns no value and may COMMIT part-way through.
A label on a PostgreSQL function (IMMUTABLE, STABLE or VOLATILE) promising how predictable its result is, which tells the planner what it may optimise.
In PostgreSQL, a packaged add-on (new types, functions or index types) installed into a database with CREATE EXTENSION, such as PostGIS or pg_trgm.
PostgreSQL's tool for making a logical backup of one database; pg_dumpall does every database plus the roles.
PostgreSQL's tool for loading a backup made by pg_dump in custom or directory format, all of it or chosen tables.
A backup saved as the SQL and data needed to rebuild the tables, as made by pg_dump. Portable across versions, but slower to restore than copying data files.
A backup that copies the database server's data files themselves. Fast to restore, but only to the same PostgreSQL major version.
One kind of index structure in PostgreSQL: B-tree, Hash, GIN, GiST, SP-GiST or BRIN. Each is good at answering different kinds of conditions.
The part of an index definition that says which operators it can speed up for a type, e.g. jsonb_path_ops makes a GIN index answer only @>.
A three-character piece of text: 'cat' gives '  c', ' ca', 'cat', 'at '. The pg_trgm extension indexes trigrams so LIKE '%text%' searches can use an index.
A PostgreSQL type holding a span of values in one column, such as a booking from 10:00 to 12:00 (tstzrange) or a set of dates (daterange).
A rule saying no two rows may 'clash' by operators you choose, e.g. the same room with overlapping times. Like UNIQUE, PostgreSQL checks it on every write.
PostgreSQL's full-text search form of a document: its words reduced to base forms (lexemes) with their positions, ready to match against a tsquery.
PostgreSQL's form of a full-text search condition, such as words that must all appear, or one word or another.
A word reduced to its base form for searching, so 'running' and 'runs' both become 'run'.
Cutting words back to a common base form ('running', 'runs' to 'run') so a search for one finds the others.
A very common word such as 'the' or 'and' that full-text search leaves out because it says nothing about the topic.
A column whose value the database computes from other columns of the same row whenever the row is written, e.g. a total from price and quantity.
PostgreSQL's built-in background helper that runs VACUUM and ANALYZE on tables automatically once enough rows have changed.
A small per-table record of which pages contain only rows every transaction can see. It lets VACUUM skip those pages and queries answer from an index alone.
VACUUM's marking of old rows as visible to everyone forever, so PostgreSQL no longer needs their transaction ID. Needed before the ID counter wraps round.
In PostgreSQL, the ID of the transaction that created a row version (xmax: the one that deleted it). The 'xmin horizon' is the oldest one still in use; VACUUM can't clean newer rows.
An option of SELECT ... FOR UPDATE that passes over rows other transactions have locked instead of waiting for them; used to build job queues.
A PostgreSQL view with one row per connection: who it is, what it's running, since when, and what it's waiting for.
A PostgreSQL feature that filters which rows each role may see or change, by rules (policies) the database adds to every query on the table.
A PostgreSQL extension that keeps running totals for every distinct query: how often it ran, total and average time, rows and data read.
In PostgreSQL, the main storage of a table: a file of 8 kB pages holding its rows in no particular order. Indexes point into it.
PostgreSQL's word for one stored version of a row. An UPDATE writes a new tuple and marks the old one as expired.
A small slot at the start of a PostgreSQL page saying where in the page each row version begins.
A row version's physical address in PostgreSQL: (page number, slot on the page). It changes whenever the row is updated, so never use it as a key.
PostgreSQL's way of storing large values: it compresses them and, if they are still big, moves them into a side table in chunks, leaving a pointer in the row.
A heap-only tuple update: when no indexed column changes and the new row version fits on the same page, PostgreSQL skips adding new index entries.
A table or index setting for how full PostgreSQL packs each page (100% by default for tables). Leaving room helps updates stay on the same page.
Copying each finished file of PostgreSQL's write-ahead log to safe storage, so a backup can later be rolled forward to any moment.
In PostgreSQL, the server process that serves one client connection. Each connection gets its own.
A small program that sits between apps and PostgreSQL and shares a few real database connections among many app connections.
PostgreSQL's setting for how much memory it keeps as its own cache of table and index pages, shared by all connections.
PostgreSQL's setting for how much memory one sort or hash step of a query may use before it spills to disk. A query can have several such steps.
A popular PostgreSQL extension that adds map and geometry types and functions: points, shapes, distances and 'what's nearby' searches.
A PostgreSQL extension that stores lists of numbers representing meaning (embeddings) and finds the most similar ones, for AI-style search.

concepts.name: Installing PostgreSQL and psql
concepts.summary: Get a PostgreSQL server running on your computer, connect to it with psql and find your way around.
concepts.why: psql is the tool every PostgreSQL tutorial uses, and a server on your own computer is a safe place to learn.
concepts.body:
Working with PostgreSQL involves two programs. The **PostgreSQL server** owns the data: it keeps the database files on disk and waits for clients to connect. **psql** is a client: you type SQL into it, it sends the SQL to the server and prints the answer.

The server and its clients don't have to be on the same computer. A client finds the server by the computer's address plus a **port**: a numbered door on a computer that network traffic is addressed to, so one machine can offer many services. PostgreSQL uses port 5432 unless told otherwise. When the server is on your own computer, its address is simply `localhost`, meaning 'this computer'.

Ways to get a server running on your own computer:

- **An installer**: the EDB installer on Windows, or Postgres.app on a Mac. The server then starts by itself.
- **A package manager**, an app store you use by typing commands: `brew install postgresql@18` (Homebrew on a Mac) or `apt install postgresql` on Linux.
- **Docker**, if you already use it (see the example).

For real applications many teams rent a **managed** PostgreSQL instead (Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL, Azure, Neon, Supabase): the provider runs the server, its backups and upgrades.

You start psql from a **terminal**: the text window where you type commands instead of clicking icons (Terminal on a Mac, PowerShell on Windows). `psql -h localhost -U postgres` means 'connect to the server on this computer as the user called postgres'. psql asks for the password, then shows its **prompt**, `postgres=#`: a short text meaning it is waiting for you (`postgres` is the database you're in).

At the prompt you type SQL ending with `;`. You can also type **meta-commands**: short commands starting with a backslash that psql handles itself instead of sending them to the server. `\l` lists databases, `\c shop` switches to the database called shop, `\dt` lists tables, `\d name` describes one table, `\?` shows help and `\q` quits.

A fresh installation has one database called `postgres` and one user, also called `postgres`. PostgreSQL calls users **roles**. This one is a **superuser**: a role that skips every permission check. Create a database per project instead of working in `postgres`, and give your apps a less powerful role (a later lesson shows how).
concepts.code:
# In a terminal: connect to the server on this computer as the user postgres
psql -h localhost -U postgres          # asks for the password

# (With Docker, this one line starts a throwaway server instead of installing one:
#  docker run --name pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:18)

# postgres=# SELECT version();
# postgres=# CREATE DATABASE shop;
# postgres=# \c shop
# You are now connected to database "shop" as user "postgres".
# shop=# CREATE TABLE product (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text);
# shop=# \dt
#          List of relations
#  Schema |  Name   | Type  |  Owner
#  public | product | table | postgres
# shop=# \q
takeaways: The server owns the data; psql and your apps are clients that connect to it
Backslash meta-commands (\l, \c, \dt, \d) are handled by psql, not sent to the server as SQL
Use a separate database per project, and don't let apps connect as the superuser
pitfalls: Forgetting the semicolon: psql keeps waiting for more input and the prompt changes to postgres-#.

quiz.q: Which of these is handled by psql itself rather than sent to the server as SQL?
quiz.explain: Backslash meta-commands are handled by psql itself, which looks up the answer for you; the others are SQL the server runs.

concepts.name: psql productivity
concepts.summary: Use psql's describe commands, wide-row display, timing, variables and SQL files to explore and work faster.
concepts.why: Knowing psql well makes exploring an unfamiliar database, or checking on a live one, much faster than clicking through a graphical app.
concepts.body:
psql is more than a place to type SQL. A handful of meta-commands save a lot of time. The **describe** family shows what a database contains:

- `\d orders` shows a table's columns, indexes and constraints; `\d+ orders` adds sizes.
- `\dn` lists schemas, `\du` roles, `\df` functions, `\di` indexes.
- Add a pattern to narrow a list: `\dt sales.*` lists only the tables in the schema called sales.

Three display helpers: `\x auto` shows each column on its own line when a row is too wide for the screen; `\pset null '(null)'` prints NULLs visibly instead of as blanks; `\timing on` prints how long each statement took.

You can save statements in a file ending in `.sql`, called a **script**, and run it with `\i file.sql` inside psql, or from the terminal with `psql -f file.sql`. Add `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` so psql stops at the first statement that fails. Without it, psql reports the error and carries on with the rest.

psql can also remember values for you. `\set id 42` stores 42 under the name `id` (a **variable**), and `:id` pastes it into SQL: `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = :id;`. Write `:'name'` to paste it as a quoted string.

Other handy ones: `\e` opens the last query in a text editor so you can fix a long statement; `\watch 2` re-runs the last query every two seconds, useful for keeping an eye on something that changes; `\o result.txt` sends results to a file instead of the screen.

A setting you change with SQL's `SET` command lasts only for your **session**: from the moment you connect until you disconnect. Settings you want every time go in a file called `.psqlrc` in your home folder, which psql runs each time it starts.

Curious how `\d` finds its answers? `\set ECHO_HIDDEN on` shows the queries it runs against the **system catalogs**: the built-in tables where PostgreSQL keeps its list of tables, columns and everything else.
concepts.code:
# ~/.psqlrc  (the file psql runs at start-up)
\set QUIET 1
\x auto
\timing on
\pset null '(null)'
\set ON_ERROR_STOP on
\set QUIET 0

# from the terminal: run a file of SQL, stopping at the first error
psql -h localhost -U app -d shop -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f migrate.sql

# inside psql
# shop=# \set uid 42
# shop=# SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = :uid;
# shop=# SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity \watch 5
#   (pg_stat_activity lists open connections; \watch re-runs it every 5 seconds)
takeaways: \d, \d+, \dn, \du, \df and \di describe what a database contains
\x auto and \timing on belong in every .psqlrc
Run SQL files with -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 so a failure stops the run
pitfalls: Running psql -f from an automated job without ON_ERROR_STOP, so a failed statement is skipped and the job still reports success.

quiz.q: You run psql -f migrate.sql and statement 3 of 10 fails. Without ON_ERROR_STOP, what happens?
options: psql reports the error and continues with statements 4 to 10
psql stops and rolls back everything
quiz.explain: By default psql prints the error and carries on, which is why automation should set ON_ERROR_STOP.

concepts.name: Clusters, databases and schemas
concepts.summary: How one PostgreSQL server holds several databases, each database holds schemas, and search_path decides which schema a name means.
concepts.why: This layout decides what each query can see, and it is the basis of permissions and of keeping different customers' data apart.
concepts.body:
In the SQL lessons, a schema meant the overall design of a database. PostgreSQL also uses the word for something concrete, so let's go through how it organises things, from the outside in.

A **cluster** is one running PostgreSQL server together with all the data it manages. Despite the name, it is not a group of computers. One cluster holds several databases, plus the roles (users), which all its databases share.

A **database** is sealed off from the others. A connection belongs to exactly one database and can't read tables in another. Give separate applications separate databases.

A **schema** is a named folder *inside* a database that holds tables, views and functions. Tables in different schemas of the same database can be joined freely. Every database starts with a schema called `public`. Writing `sales.orders` means 'the orders table in the schema sales'.

When you write just `orders`, PostgreSQL looks it up using the **search_path** setting: a list of schemas to try in order. The default, `"$user", public`, means first a schema named after your role (if one exists), then `public`. So `SELECT * FROM orders` finds `public.orders`. Writing the schema name, as in `sales.orders`, always works.

Schemas are handy to group the areas of an application (`billing`, `audit`), or to give each customer of a shared app a folder of their own. Since PostgreSQL 15, ordinary roles can't create tables in `public` unless the database's owner allows it with `GRANT CREATE`, so it's common to create your own schema.

To change search_path for good, set it per role (`ALTER ROLE app SET search_path = app, public`) or per database, rather than with `SET` every time you connect.
takeaways: Server (cluster) > database > schema > table
A connection sees one database; schemas inside it can be joined freely
search_path decides which schema a name without a schema prefix refers to
pitfalls: Expecting one query to combine tables from two different databases.

quiz.q: search_path is billing, public and both schemas have a table called invoice. What does SELECT * FROM invoice read?
quiz.explain: Names resolve to the first schema in search_path that contains a matching object.

concepts.name: Connecting applications
concepts.summary: How apps find and log in to PostgreSQL: drivers, connection URIs, and the server rules that accept or refuse a connection.
concepts.why: Most 'can't connect' problems come down to the connection URI, the server's access rules or the encryption settings covered here.
concepts.body:
Programs you write, such as a website's code, are clients too. They don't type into psql; they use a **driver**: a ready-made piece of code for your programming language that knows how to talk to PostgreSQL. Examples: psycopg (Python), pg (Node.js), pgx (Go), JDBC (Java), Npgsql (.NET).

Almost every driver accepts the connection details as one line of text, a **connection URI**, built like a web address: `postgresql://user:password@host:5432/dbname?sslmode=require`. Read it left to right: user name and password, the computer the server runs on, the port, the database, then options after the `?`.

Passwords don't belong in code. psql and the other PostgreSQL tools also read settings from **environment variables**: named settings your terminal hands to every program it starts, such as `PGHOST`, `PGUSER`, `PGDATABASE` and `PGPASSWORD`. A file called `.pgpass` in your home folder can hold passwords, so they never appear in the commands you type.

On the server, two settings decide whether a connection gets in. The first is `listen_addresses`, in the server's settings file `postgresql.conf`. Many installations default to `localhost`, so only programs on the same computer can connect; the official Docker setup accepts connections from anywhere.

The second is `pg_hba.conf`, a list of rules read from top to bottom. Each rule names a connection type, database, user and client address, plus how the user must prove who they are (**authentication**): `scram-sha-256` means with a password, `peer` means 'same user name as on this computer'. The first rule that matches wins. After editing the file, reload the server with `SELECT pg_reload_conf();`.

Never build SQL by pasting values into its text. Put a placeholder such as `%s` where each value goes and hand the values to the driver separately, as in the example. The driver sends them apart from the SQL, so a value can never be run as SQL.

Three more habits. Give each application its own role with only the rights it needs. Use `sslmode=require` (or the stricter `verify-full`) for any connection that crosses a network, so the traffic is encrypted. And keep connections few: each one costs the server a separate running program, a **process**. So apps keep a few connections open and reuse them, a **connection pool**, instead of opening a new one for every visitor.
concepts.code:
# Python, using the psycopg driver (install it with: pip install "psycopg[binary]")
import psycopg

url = "postgresql://app:secret@localhost:5432/shop"
with psycopg.connect(url) as conn:              # connect; commits when the block ends
    with conn.cursor() as cur:                  # cur sends SQL and reads results
        cur.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS note ("
                    "id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, body text)")
        # %s is a placeholder; the value travels separately from the SQL
        cur.execute("INSERT INTO note (body) VALUES (%s)", ("hello",))
        cur.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM note WHERE body = %s", ("hello",))
        print(cur.fetchone()[0])               # 1

# pg_hba.conf line: let role app reach database shop from the 10.0.0.x network
# with a password
# host  shop  app  10.0.0.0/24  scram-sha-256
takeaways: Connection URI: postgresql://user:pass@host:port/db?sslmode=...
pg_hba.conf rules are matched top to bottom; reload the server after changes
Pass values to the driver separately with placeholders, never by pasting them into the SQL text
pitfalls: Pasting values typed by users straight into the SQL text, which lets an attacker slip in SQL of their own (SQL injection).

quiz.q: A client gets 'no pg_hba.conf entry for host'. What needs to change?
options: A rule in pg_hba.conf allowing that host, user and database
quiz.explain: The server reached authentication but found no matching pg_hba.conf rule for that connection.

concepts.name: Choosing core data types
concepts.summary: Pick PostgreSQL types well: text vs varchar, integer sizes, numeric vs float, boolean and bytea.
concepts.why: Types are hard to change once a table is big, and the right ones prevent mistakes such as rounding errors in money.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL has more data types than most databases, but a few choices cover most columns.

- **Text**: use `text`. `varchar(n)` is the same type with a length check, and `char(n)` pads values with spaces, so avoid it. If you need a limit, `CHECK (length(x) <= n)` is easier to change later. Speed is identical.
- **Whole numbers**: `integer` (4 bytes, up to about 2.1 billion) and `bigint` (8 bytes). Use `bigint` for the ids of tables that may grow large; running out of `integer` ids is a classic outage. `smallint` rarely pays off.
- **Exact decimals**: `numeric(p, s)` for money and anything that must add up exactly. `real` and `double precision` are floating-point numbers: fast but approximate, fine for measurements. Avoid the `money` type; how it behaves depends on a server setting.
- **Yes/no**: `boolean` holds `true`, `false` or `NULL`.
- **Raw bytes**: `bytea` holds any bytes, such as a small image. For large files, keep the file in a file-storage service (such as Amazon S3) and store only its location.
- **Dates and times**: `date`, and `timestamptz` (next lessons).

Also useful, and covered later: `uuid`, arrays (several values in one column), `inet` for IP addresses (the numeric addresses computers use on a network, like 203.0.113.7), and range types.

To convert a value to another type, use `::` or the standard `CAST`: `'42'::int` turns the text '42' into the number 42. `pg_typeof(expr)` tells you the type of any expression, which is handy when PostgreSQL complains that an operator doesn't exist for your types.
takeaways: text everywhere; add a CHECK if you need a max length
bigint for ids that may grow; numeric for money
Floats are approximate; never compare them for exact equality
pitfalls: Using integer primary keys on a fast-growing table and hitting 2,147,483,647.

quiz.q: Which type should store invoice totals?
quiz.explain: numeric does exact decimal arithmetic; floats round, and money depends on a server setting.

concepts.name: Identity columns and UUIDs
concepts.summary: Generate keys with GENERATED AS IDENTITY instead of serial, or with gen_random_uuid() and uuidv7().
concepts.why: Every table needs a way to make new keys, and the modern options avoid the quirks of the older serial type.
concepts.body:
In the SQL lessons you met identity columns, which number new rows automatically. PostgreSQL offers two flavours:

- `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` rejects a value you type in yourself, unless you add `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`. That protects against accidental hand-made ids.
- `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` uses the next number unless you supply one, which is convenient when copying rows in from another system.

Older code uses `serial` and `bigserial` instead. They aren't real types but a shorthand that sets up a separate counter plus a default value, which causes quirks with permissions and when copying table definitions. Prefer identity columns in new tables.

Both are powered by a **sequence**: a counter stored in the database that hands out the next number each time it's asked. To stay fast, it doesn't wait for transactions to finish and never takes a number back. So a rolled-back insert still uses up its number, and ids have **gaps**. Never rely on ids being consecutive, or use them as a count.

For **UUIDs**, use the `uuid` type: 16 bytes, where the same value as text takes more than twice that. `gen_random_uuid()` makes random ones. PostgreSQL 18 adds `uuidv7()`, whose values begin with the current time, so new ones sort after older ones.

That matters for the index behind a primary key, which keeps its values in sorted order. Values that only grow are always added at the end, which is cheap. Random values land all over the index, which is slower and wastes space on large tables. So prefer `uuidv7()` when you choose UUIDs as keys.

If you load rows with ids you chose yourself, move the sequence past the largest one with `setval`, or the next automatic id will collide with an existing row.
takeaways: Prefer GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY over serial
Sequences never roll back, so ids have gaps
Store UUIDs in the uuid type; uuidv7() keeps inserts index-friendly
pitfalls: Storing UUIDs as text, which doubles their size and slows comparisons.

quiz.q: A transaction inserts a row into an identity table and then rolls back. What happens to the generated id?
options: It is reused by the next insert
It is consumed, leaving a gap
quiz.explain: A sequence never takes a number back, even when the transaction that used it is rolled back.

concepts.name: Timestamps and time zones
concepts.summary: Store moments in time as timestamptz, understand the TimeZone setting, and do interval arithmetic.
concepts.why: Time zone mistakes are among the most common data errors; one rule about timestamptz prevents most of them.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL has two timestamp types, and their names mislead:

- `timestamp with time zone`, or **timestamptz**, stores one exact moment, kept internally in UTC. Each connection (a **session**) has a `TimeZone` setting. A value you type without an offset like `+04` is read in that time zone, and values are shown converted to it. The original zone is *not* stored.
- `timestamp` (without time zone) stores a clock reading with no zone at all. `2026-03-29 02:30` means nothing until you say where.

Rule: use **timestamptz** for events that happened at a moment (created_at, paid_at). Use `timestamp`, or `date` plus `time`, only for local times that must not shift, such as 'the shop opens at 09:00 local time', and store the zone's name in another column.

Useful tools:

- `now()` returns the time the current transaction started; `clock_timestamp()` the actual current time.
- `AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Yerevan'` turns a timestamptz into the local clock time in that zone (and the reverse for a plain timestamp).
- An `interval` is a length of time: `now() - interval '7 days'` is a week ago, and `age(a, b)` gives the time between two moments.
- `date_trunc('day', ts)` rounds down to the start of the day (or hour, month...), in the session's time zone, for grouping by day.

Set the server's or database's `TimeZone` to UTC, and convert to local time only when showing values to people, in the application or with `AT TIME ZONE`.
takeaways: timestamptz stores an instant (UTC) and displays it in the session TimeZone
Use timestamptz for events; plain timestamp only for local times that must not shift
AT TIME ZONE converts between exact moments and local clock times
pitfalls: Using timestamp without time zone for created_at and getting shifted values when servers or sessions change zone.

quiz.q: A timestamptz column holds 12:00 UTC. A session with TimeZone = 'Europe/Paris' (UTC+1 in winter) selects it in January. What is shown?
quiz.explain: The same instant is displayed converted to the session's time zone.

concepts.name: RETURNING and upserts
concepts.summary: Get generated values back from INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE with RETURNING, and combine it with ON CONFLICT.
concepts.why: RETURNING saves a second query, and replaces 'insert, then select it back' code that can pick up the wrong row when many people write at once.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL's `RETURNING` clause makes statements that change data hand back rows, like a `SELECT` of what they just changed:

- `INSERT ... RETURNING id` gives you generated ids and default values without a second query.
- `UPDATE ... RETURNING *` shows the new values after the update.
- `DELETE ... RETURNING *` returns what was removed, handy for moving rows to an archive table.

PostgreSQL 18 also lets you write `RETURNING old.col, new.col` to see both the before and after values of an update.

It pairs well with an **upsert**: insert a row, or update it if a row with the same key already exists. In PostgreSQL that's `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`. `ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col` does it as one step that nobody else can sneak in between. `EXCLUDED` means the row you tried to insert.

`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` skips duplicates instead. Note that `RETURNING` then gives no row for the ones it skipped.

A statement that changes data can also sit inside a `WITH` clause at the start of a query, and the rest of the query can use its `RETURNING` rows like a table. That lets you, for example, delete old rows and copy them into an archive table in a single statement.

`ON CONFLICT` needs a unique index or `UNIQUE` constraint on the columns you name. It is the safe replacement for 'SELECT to check, then INSERT if missing', which breaks when two people do it at the same moment.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE stock (sku text PRIMARY KEY, qty int NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE stock_archive (sku text, qty int, archived_at timestamptz DEFAULT now());

INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('A1', 5) RETURNING *;            -- A1 | 5

INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('A1', 3)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty
RETURNING sku, qty;                                         -- A1 | 8

UPDATE stock SET qty = 0 WHERE sku = 'A1' RETURNING qty;    -- 0

WITH gone AS (
    DELETE FROM stock WHERE qty = 0 RETURNING sku, qty
)
INSERT INTO stock_archive (sku, qty) SELECT sku, qty FROM gone
RETURNING sku;                                              -- A1
takeaways: RETURNING makes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE hand back the rows they changed
ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE with EXCLUDED is a one-step upsert
A data-changing statement inside WITH can feed the rest of the query
pitfalls: Expecting RETURNING to produce a row for inputs skipped by ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.

quiz.q: In ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, what is EXCLUDED?
options: The row already in the table
The row that was proposed for insertion
quiz.explain: EXCLUDED holds the values you tried to insert; the table name refers to the existing row.

concepts.name: Bulk loading with COPY
concepts.summary: Load and export CSV files fast with COPY on the server, or with \copy from psql.
concepts.why: COPY is many times faster than one INSERT per row for loading data in, getting it out, and bulk fixes.
concepts.body:
A **CSV** file is a table saved as plain text: one row per line, with values separated by commas. Spreadsheet apps open and save it. `COPY` moves data between a table (or a query's result) and such a file in one operation.

It's the fastest way to load lots of rows, often many times faster than separate `INSERT` statements, because the server doesn't have to read and plan a new statement for every row, and the client doesn't wait for a reply after each one.

Two versions look alike but run in different places:

- `COPY table FROM '/path/file.csv'` runs **on the server**. The path means a file on the database server's own disk, and only a superuser or a role given special rights (`pg_read_server_files`) may use it. It's no use with a managed database, whose computer you can't reach.
- `\copy table FROM 'file.csv'` is a psql meta-command. psql reads the file on *your* computer and sends its contents to the server over the connection. Same options, no special rights. This is usually what you want.

Common options: `(FORMAT csv, HEADER true)` for a file whose first line holds column names, `DELIMITER` for another separator, `NULL ''` to read empty values as NULL, and a column list to load only some columns. To export a query's result: `\copy (SELECT ...) TO 'out.csv' (FORMAT csv, HEADER)`.

`COPY` is all-or-nothing: one bad row cancels the whole load. (PostgreSQL 17 added `ON_ERROR ignore` to skip rows whose values don't fit their types.) For messy files, load into a **staging table** first: a temporary table whose columns are all `text`, so every row fits. Clean the data with SQL, then copy it into the real table with `INSERT ... SELECT`.

Drivers offer COPY too, for example `cursor.copy()` in psycopg 3.
concepts.code:
# products.csv
# sku,name,price
# A1,Pen,1.50
# B2,Notebook,4.00

# in psql, connected to the shop database:
CREATE TABLE product (sku text PRIMARY KEY, name text, price numeric(8,2));
\copy product FROM 'products.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)
SELECT count(*) FROM product;
-- 2
\copy (SELECT sku, price * 1.2 AS price_vat FROM product) TO 'vat.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)
takeaways: COPY is the fast path for bulk import and export
COPY reads files on the server; \copy reads them on your computer
Load messy data into a staging table of text columns, then clean it with SQL
pitfalls: Using server-side COPY with a path on your laptop and getting 'could not open file'.

quiz.q: You're connected with psql to a managed database and want to load data.csv from your laptop. What do you use?
quiz.explain: \copy sends the file from your computer over the connection; COPY looks for the path on the server's own disk.

concepts.name: Roles and privileges
concepts.summary: Create login and group roles, GRANT each only the privileges it needs, and set default privileges for tables created later.
concepts.why: Giving each role only the rights it needs limits the damage of a leaked password or a security hole in the app.
concepts.body:
In PostgreSQL, users and groups are both **roles**. A role with `LOGIN` can connect; a role without it acts as a group that other roles are made members of, and members get its rights. Roles belong to the whole cluster, so every database on the server shares them.

A right on something is a **privilege**, given with `GRANT` and taken away with `REVOKE`. Privileges are granted on databases, schemas, tables and so on:

- `GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE shop TO app;`
- `GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA app TO app;`, needed to reach anything inside the schema.
- `GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA app TO app;`
- `GRANT USAGE ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA app TO app;` so inserts can use the counters behind auto-numbered `serial` columns.

`ON ALL TABLES` only covers tables that exist now. For tables created later, use `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES`. It applies to tables created later *by the role that runs it* (or by the role named in `FOR ROLE owner`).

A clean pattern: an **owner** role (`app_owner`, no login) owns the schema and runs migrations. Group roles `app_rw` and `app_ro` hold read-write and read-only privileges. Login roles for services and people are members of those groups. Don't let the application connect as the owner or as a superuser: owners can drop tables, and superusers skip every check, including row-level security (a later lesson).

Since PostgreSQL 14, the built-in roles `pg_read_all_data` and `pg_write_all_data` make read-only reporting users easy. Use `\du` and `\dp` in psql to inspect roles and table privileges.
takeaways: Users and groups are both roles; LOGIN makes a role a user
Schema USAGE plus table privileges are both needed
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES covers tables created in the future
pitfalls: Granting on ALL TABLES once and wondering why new tables are inaccessible.

quiz.q: A role has SELECT on app.orders but queries fail with 'permission denied for schema app'. What's missing?
quiz.explain: Objects inside a schema can't be reached without USAGE on the schema itself.

concepts.name: jsonb in practice
concepts.summary: Store JSON in jsonb columns, and query, update and index it with ->, ->>, @>, jsonb_set and the SQL/JSON functions.
concepts.why: jsonb lets one relational database also hold flexible, document-shaped data without running a second system.
concepts.body:
**JSON** is a text format for structured data: `{"plan": "pro", "tags": ["beta", "vip"]}` holds named values (keys) in curly braces and lists in square brackets, and they can nest. Apps and web services exchange data in it constantly.

PostgreSQL has two JSON types. `json` stores the text exactly as given. **jsonb** stores it already taken apart into a compact form (duplicate keys removed, spacing dropped) that is faster to query and can be indexed. Use `jsonb`.

Reading:

- `doc -> 'key'` returns jsonb; `doc ->> 'key'` returns text. Chain them, `doc -> 'address' ->> 'city'`, or use a path: `doc #>> '{address,city}'`.
- `doc @> '{"plan": "pro"}'` tests whether the document contains that piece, and can use a GIN index (an index type for values that hold many items; see the Advanced lesson on index types).
- `doc ? 'key'` tests whether a top-level key exists.
- `jsonb_array_elements(doc -> 'items')` turns a JSON list into rows; `jsonb_to_recordset` turns a list of `{...}` items into rows with typed columns.
- SQL/JSON paths: `jsonb_path_query(doc, '$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 1)')`; PostgreSQL 17 adds the standard `JSON_TABLE`.

Writing: `jsonb_set(doc, '{address,city}', '"Gyumri"')` replaces a nested value, `doc || '{"vip": true}'` merges in top-level keys, and `doc - 'key'` removes one. Each update rewrites the whole value, so large documents that change often are costly.

Use jsonb for data whose shape really varies: optional extra details, data received from other services, settings. Anything you filter, join or check regularly deserves a real column, with a type, constraints, and the statistics the query planner relies on.
takeaways: -> returns jsonb, ->> returns text
@> containment queries can use a GIN index
Move values you filter on often into real columns
pitfalls: Comparing profile -> 'age' > 30: -> returns jsonb, so cast (profile ->> 'age')::int instead.

quiz.q: What does profile ->> 'plan' return for {"plan": "pro"}?
quiz.explain: ->> extracts the field as text; -> would return the jsonb string "pro".

concepts.name: Arrays, enums and domains
concepts.summary: Use array columns with ANY and unnest, enum types for fixed value sets, and domains for reusable constraints.
concepts.why: These PostgreSQL types model common patterns concisely, as long as you know where each one stops fitting.
concepts.body:
**Arrays**: a column can hold a list of values of one type, written `text[]` or `int[]`. Write a value as `'{a,b}'` or `ARRAY['a','b']`.

Useful operators: `'x' = ANY(tags)` (is x one of the items?), `tags @> ARRAY['x']` (contains; can use a GIN index), `&&` (any item in common), `array_length(tags, 1)`, and `unnest(tags)`, which turns an array into rows; `array_agg` goes the other way. Positions start at 1.

Arrays suit small lists you read together, such as tags. If each item must point to a row in another table (a foreign key) or carry details of its own, use a separate table with one row per item instead.

**Enums**: a type with a fixed list of allowed values, `CREATE TYPE mood AS ENUM ('sad', 'ok', 'happy')`. Values are stored compactly and sort in the order you listed them. You can add values (`ALTER TYPE mood ADD VALUE 'ecstatic' AFTER 'happy'`), but removing or renaming one is awkward. For lists that change often, a lookup table or a `CHECK` constraint is more flexible.

**Domains**: a named type with rules attached, reusable across tables: `CREATE DOMAIN email AS text CHECK (VALUE ~ '^[^@]+@[^@]+$')` (the `~` tests the value against a text pattern). Change the rule in one place and every column using the domain follows.

All three are PostgreSQL additions to standard SQL (arrays partly standard), so they tie you a little more to PostgreSQL, which is usually a fine trade.
takeaways: Arrays: = ANY(), @>, && and unnest; 1-based
Enums sort in declaration order and are hard to shrink
Domains are reusable constrained types
pitfalls: Storing a list of ids in an array instead of a linking table (a junction table), and losing foreign-key checks.

quiz.q: Which query finds tickets whose tags include 'bug'?
quiz.explain: = ANY(array) tests whether any element equals the value.

concepts.name: Partial, expression and concurrent indexes
concepts.summary: Build indexes without stopping writes, index calculated values and subsets of rows, and find indexes nobody uses.
concepts.why: These options make indexes smaller, more targeted and safe to add to a table a live app is using.
concepts.body:
A plain `CREATE INDEX` stops all writes to the table until it finishes, which can take minutes or hours on a big table. On the live system real users rely on (**production**), use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. It builds the index while inserts, updates and deletes carry on, at the cost of taking longer and reading the table twice. It can't run inside a transaction block, and if it fails it leaves an `INVALID` index that you must drop before trying again. `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` exist too.

An **expression index** indexes a calculated value, so queries using the same calculation can use it: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` serves `WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com'`. The query must use exactly the same expression.

A **partial index** includes only the rows matching a `WHERE` condition: `CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'` stays tiny when most orders are completed. A partial *unique* index enforces uniqueness on just those rows, for example one active subscription per user.

`INCLUDE (cols)` stores extra columns in an index so some queries never need to read the table (a **covering index**).

To find dead weight, check `pg_stat_user_indexes`: an index whose `idx_scan` count stays at 0 for weeks is a candidate to drop. If the database has copies on other servers (replicas), check those too; each keeps its own counts. Every index slows writes and takes memory, so keep the set lean.
takeaways: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY doesn't stop writes; drop any INVALID leftovers
Expression indexes need the query to use the same expression
Partial indexes are small and can enforce uniqueness on a subset of rows
pitfalls: Running CREATE INDEX (without CONCURRENTLY) on a large, busy table during business hours.

quiz.q: An index exists on lower(email). Which WHERE clause can use it?
quiz.explain: Only a condition on the identical expression lower(email) can use the expression index.

concepts.name: EXPLAIN ANALYZE with BUFFERS
concepts.summary: Read PostgreSQL plans with timings and buffer counts, spot bad row estimates, and catch slow plans with auto_explain.
concepts.why: Buffers show how much data a query touches, which is usually the real cost behind slow queries.
concepts.body:
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` runs the query and shows, for each step of the plan, the estimated and actual row counts, the time taken, and **buffers**. PostgreSQL stores and reads data in 8 kB blocks called **pages**, and the buffer counts say how many pages each step touched. From PostgreSQL 18, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows buffers by default.

`shared hit` counts pages found in PostgreSQL's own memory cache. `read` counts pages it had to ask the operating system for, which may mean reading the disk.

How to read a plan:

- Read it inside-out: the most indented steps run first and feed the ones above them.
- `actual time=a..b` is in milliseconds for one run of that step. A step that runs repeatedly shows `loops=N`, so multiply.
- Compare estimated and actual `rows=`. Off by 10x or more points to stale statistics or a condition the planner can't estimate.
- A large `Rows Removed by Filter` compared with the rows returned suggests a missing or unusable index.

Two more signs:

- A sort, or a hash step (which builds a lookup table in memory), that didn't fit in memory shows `external merge Disk:` or `Batches:` above 1. That means `work_mem`, the memory each such step may use, is too small for this query.
- Many `read` buffers means the data wasn't cached yet, or the query simply touches too much data.

For big plans, use `FORMAT JSON` and a viewer such as explain.dalibo.com or pgMustard. To catch slow queries on the live system that you can't reproduce, turn on **auto_explain**, an add-on that ships with PostgreSQL: set `auto_explain.log_min_duration` and it writes the plan of every slower statement to the server's log.

Remember that `ANALYZE` really runs the statement: wrap an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` in `BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;`.
takeaways: BUFFERS shows pages from cache (hit) and from disk (read)
Big estimate-vs-actual gaps and large Rows Removed by Filter point to the fix
auto_explain logs plans of slow queries in production
pitfalls: Timing a query twice and trusting the second, cached run as representative.

quiz.q: A Sort node shows 'Sort Method: external merge Disk: 120MB'. What does it suggest?
options: The sort exceeded work_mem and spilled to disk
quiz.explain: External merge means the data to sort didn't fit in work_mem for that operation.

concepts.name: Transactions in PostgreSQL
concepts.summary: Undoable schema changes, savepoints, failed transactions, and time limits that protect the server from stuck connections.
concepts.why: PostgreSQL's transactions behave differently from other databases in ways that affect migrations and how apps handle errors.
concepts.body:
A few PostgreSQL behaviours to know beyond `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`.

**Schema changes can be rolled back.** `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE` and most other DDL take part in transactions. A migration wrapped in a transaction either fully applies or leaves no trace, a big advantage over MySQL. Exceptions include `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `VACUUM` (the cleanup command; see the Advanced lesson) and `CREATE DATABASE`.

**An error spoils the transaction.** After any error inside a transaction, every further statement fails with "current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block" until you `ROLLBACK`.

**Savepoints** let you recover part-way: `SAVEPOINT s1; ... ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1;` undoes only the work after the savepoint and clears the error. Database drivers use them for transactions nested inside others. Each one has a cost, so don't create one per row in a big job.

**Isolation level.** How much transactions running at the same time see of each other's changes is set by the **isolation level**. The default, Read Committed, lets each statement see everything committed before it began. Stricter levels (`BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ` or `SERIALIZABLE`) may cancel a transaction with error code `40001`, which means 'run it again', so the app must be ready to retry.

Protect the server with **timeouts**, limits on how long something may take, set per role or per database:

- `statement_timeout` cancels statements that run too long.
- `lock_timeout` stops a statement from waiting forever for a lock.
- `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` ends sessions that opened a transaction and then went quiet; they hold locks and stop VACUUM from cleaning up.
- `transaction_timeout` (PostgreSQL 17) caps a whole transaction.
takeaways: Most DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL
After an error, ROLLBACK (or roll back to a savepoint) before continuing
Set statement, lock and idle-in-transaction timeouts
pitfalls: Catching an error in app code and carrying on with the same transaction, which PostgreSQL has already marked as aborted.

quiz.q: Inside BEGIN ... you run CREATE TABLE x and then ROLLBACK. What happens to x in PostgreSQL?
options: x does not exist; the DDL was rolled back
x exists but is empty and locked
quiz.explain: PostgreSQL DDL is transactional, so the CREATE TABLE is undone with the rest.

concepts.name: SQL and PL/pgSQL functions
concepts.summary: Write functions in plain SQL or in PL/pgSQL, with variables, IF, loops and errors, and procedures that can commit part-way.
concepts.why: Functions on the server keep data-heavy logic next to the data, and triggers (code the database runs automatically when rows change) are built from them.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL functions can be written in several languages. The two built-in ones:

- **SQL functions** (`LANGUAGE sql`) are one or more SQL statements; the result of the last one is returned. The planner can copy simple ones straight into the calling query, so they're as fast as writing the SQL out. Since PostgreSQL 14 you can write the body in standard form with `BEGIN ATOMIC ... END`.
- **PL/pgSQL** (`LANGUAGE plpgsql`) adds what SQL lacks: **variables** (named boxes for values, listed under `DECLARE`), `IF`, **loops** that repeat steps, `RAISE` to report errors or messages, and `EXCEPTION` blocks to catch errors. Use it when you need step-by-step logic.

Key options:

- **Volatility**, a promise about how predictable the function is: `IMMUTABLE` (the same inputs always give the same output, and it reads no tables; required for functions used in an index), `STABLE` (changes no data and gives the same result throughout one statement), `VOLATILE` (the default: no promises).
- `RETURNS TABLE (...)` or `RETURNS SETOF` to return rows; call such a function in `FROM`.
- `SECURITY DEFINER` runs the function with its owner's privileges. That's powerful, so also fix its `search_path` so nobody can slip in a look-alike table.

**Procedures** (`CREATE PROCEDURE`, run with `CALL`) differ from functions in that they can `COMMIT` part-way through. That suits big jobs that work through data in chunks, committing after each.

Keep most business rules in the application unless the logic is data-heavy or must apply to every program that writes to the table: code inside the database is harder to track, test and fix.
takeaways: LANGUAGE sql for simple functions the planner can inline; plpgsql for step-by-step logic
Mark volatility correctly; functions used in indexes must be IMMUTABLE
Procedures can COMMIT inside; functions cannot
pitfalls: Declaring a function IMMUTABLE when it reads tables, leading to stale or wrong results.

quiz.q: What happens to the first UPDATE when RAISE EXCEPTION fires inside the function?
options: It is saved in a savepoint for later
It is rolled back with the rest of the statement
Only the second UPDATE is undone
quiz.explain: An unhandled exception aborts the whole statement, undoing all its changes.

concepts.name: Materialized views
concepts.summary: Store a query's result with CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW and refresh it on a schedule, without blocking readers.
concepts.why: Materialized views make expensive reports instant without building a separate system to keep summaries up to date.
concepts.body:
A regular view is just a saved query, executed each time you select from it. A **materialized view** runs the query once and stores the result like a table, so reading it is fast — at the cost of being stale until you refresh it.

- `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales AS SELECT ...` creates and fills it (add `WITH NO DATA` to fill later).
- `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales` recomputes it from scratch. It takes a lock that blocks reads while it runs.
- `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_sales` computes the new result and applies the differences, so readers keep seeing the old data during the refresh. It requires a **unique index** on the materialized view and is slower overall.

You can index materialized views like tables, which is often the point: a pre-aggregated, indexed summary.

PostgreSQL has no built-in automatic or incremental refresh. Schedule refreshes yourself: with cron (the standard scheduler on Linux and macOS), the `pg_cron` extension or your app's job runner, and choose a frequency the business can accept as staleness. If you need always-current aggregates, maintain a summary table with triggers (code the database runs on every change) or in the application instead, or look at extensions for incremental view maintenance.

Good fits: dashboards, leaderboards, search facets, and expensive joins that change rarely compared with how often they're read.
takeaways: A materialized view stores the result and is stale until refreshed
REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY keeps it readable but needs a unique index
Schedule refreshes yourself (cron, pg_cron)
pitfalls: Expecting a materialized view to update itself when the base tables change.

quiz.q: Why might REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY fail on a new materialized view?
quiz.explain: Concurrent refresh diffs old and new rows by a unique key, so a unique index is required.

concepts.name: Backups with pg_dump and pg_restore
concepts.summary: Make logical backups with pg_dump, restore all or part of them with pg_restore, and test that restores work.
concepts.why: A backup you haven't restored is a hope, not a backup; pg_dump is the everyday tool for it.
concepts.body:
**pg_dump** makes a **logical backup** of one database: the SQL to recreate its tables plus their data, as they were at the moment it started. It reads from a frozen view of the data (a **snapshot**), so normal reads and writes carry on meanwhile.

Formats:

- **plain** (`-Fp`, the default): a file of SQL statements you run with `psql`. Readable, but you can only restore all of it.
- **custom** (`-Fc`): a compressed archive restored with **pg_restore**, which can restore chosen tables (`-t`), list the contents (`-l`) and run several restore jobs at once (`-j`). The usual choice.
- **directory** (`-Fd`): a folder with one file per table; it can also *dump* with several jobs at once (`-j 4`).

pg_dump covers one database, not the roles, which belong to the whole cluster. Dump those with `pg_dumpall --globals-only`.

Useful restore options: `--no-owner` and `--no-privileges` when the target server has different roles; `--clean --if-exists` to drop existing tables before recreating them; `-d` to choose the target database. A newer pg_restore can read dumps from older servers, which makes dump-and-restore a simple (if slow) way to move to a new major version.

Limits: for big databases, dump and restore take hours, and you can only go back to the moment of the dump. Busy production systems add **physical backups** (copies of the data files themselves) plus the server's change log (the write-ahead log), which allow restoring to any chosen minute; that's an Expert lesson. Whatever you use, **automate a regular test restore** and check the result.
concepts.code:
# custom-format dump of one database, plus cluster-wide roles
pg_dump -Fc -d shop -f shop.dump
pg_dumpall --globals-only -f globals.sql

# inspect, then restore into a fresh database with 4 parallel jobs
pg_restore -l shop.dump | head
createdb shop_restore
pg_restore -d shop_restore -j 4 --no-owner shop.dump

# restore only one table's data from the archive
pg_restore -d shop_restore -t orders --data-only shop.dump

# quick sanity check of the restore
psql -d shop_restore -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"
takeaways: pg_dump is a consistent logical backup of one database
Use -Fc (or -Fd) so pg_restore can restore chosen tables, with several jobs at once
Dump roles separately with pg_dumpall --globals-only and test restores
pitfalls: Backing up databases with pg_dump but never the roles, so after a restore the privileges name roles that don't exist.

quiz.q: Which pg_dump format lets pg_restore restore a single table and run with -j?
quiz.explain: Custom (and directory) archives are read by pg_restore, which can pick tables and run several jobs at once.

concepts.name: GIN, GiST, BRIN and operator classes
concepts.summary: Pick the right kind of index for jsonb, arrays, text search, geometry and huge append-only tables.
concepts.why: When a B-tree can't serve a query, choosing the right kind of index is the difference between seconds and milliseconds.
concepts.body:
A B-tree keeps values sorted, which serves `=`, `<`, `>` and sorting. Many PostgreSQL operators ask something else: does this list contain x, do these ranges overlap, which point is nearest? So PostgreSQL has several **index access methods**, different index structures, each with **operator classes** that say which operators it can speed up for a given type.

**GIN** (generalized inverted index) works like the index at the back of a book: for every element (an array item, a jsonb key or value, a word, a three-letter fragment) it lists the rows containing it. Use it for `@>`, `?`, `&&` and full-text search's `@@`. For jsonb, the `jsonb_path_ops` class is smaller and faster for `@>` but can't answer `?`. GIN is slower to update; it collects new entries in a pending list and adds them in bulk.

**GiST** (generalized search tree) indexes things that overlap or have a distance: map shapes (with the PostGIS extension), ranges, and nearest-first queries like `ORDER BY location <-> point`. It also powers exclusion constraints (next lesson).

**SP-GiST** suits data that divides into regions, such as points and IP address prefixes. **Hash** indexes answer only `=`.

**BRIN** (block range index) stores only the smallest and largest value for each run of table pages. It's tiny, a few kilobytes for a huge table, and works when values follow the order rows were written in, such as `created_at` in a table you only ever append to.

The **pg_trgm** extension indexes **trigrams** (three-character pieces of text) with GIN or GiST. That makes `LIKE '%term%'`, `ILIKE` and 'similar spelling' searches indexable, the usual answer to 'my contains-search is slow'.

Check which operators an index supports before creating it, and confirm with `EXPLAIN` that queries use it. Extensions such as pgvector add further index types (HNSW, IVFFlat) for finding the most similar vectors, used in AI search.
takeaways: GIN for containment in jsonb, arrays, text search and trigrams
GiST for ranges, geometry, nearest neighbour and exclusion constraints
BRIN is tiny and great for naturally ordered, append-only data
pitfalls: Creating BRIN on a column whose values are scattered randomly through the table.

quiz.q: Which index makes WHERE name ILIKE '%ova%' fast?
quiz.explain: Trigram GIN indexes break text into 3-character pieces, so substring searches can be answered from the index.

concepts.name: Range types and exclusion constraints
concepts.summary: Model intervals with tstzrange and daterange, query overlaps, and forbid overlapping bookings with EXCLUDE.
concepts.why: Double bookings happen when two people grab the same slot at the same moment; an exclusion constraint prevents them in one line.
concepts.body:
A **range type** stores an interval of values as one column: `int4range`, `numrange`, `daterange`, `tstzrange`. Bounds can be inclusive `[` or exclusive `)`; the convention `[start, end)` makes adjacent ranges meet without overlapping. Since PostgreSQL 14, **multiranges** hold sets of non-contiguous ranges.

Operators make interval logic simple and correct:

- `&&` overlaps, `@>` contains a value or range, `<@` is contained by.
- `-|-` adjacent, `*` intersection, `+` union.
- `lower(r)`, `upper(r)`, `isempty(r)`.

The killer feature is the **exclusion constraint**: `EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)` means "no two rows may have equal `room` *and* overlapping `during`". Like a UNIQUE constraint, the check and the write happen as one step, so two simultaneous bookings for the same slot can't both succeed, which checks in application code can't guarantee without locks. Using `=` on a plain column inside a GiST index needs the `btree_gist` extension.

Ranges are useful for bookings, price validity periods, shift schedules and data that keeps its history with validity periods. PostgreSQL 18 adds temporal `PRIMARY KEY`/`UNIQUE` constraints with `WITHOUT OVERLAPS`, building on the same idea.
takeaways: Range types store intervals; use [start, end) bounds
&& tests overlap, @> tests containment
EXCLUDE USING gist prevents overlapping rows atomically
pitfalls: Storing start and end in two columns and checking overlaps in application code, which fails when two bookings arrive at the same moment.

quiz.q: Ranges '[10:00, 12:00)' and '[12:00, 13:00)' for the same room. Does the exclusion constraint reject the second?
options: No, the first excludes 12:00 so they don't overlap
Only if the ranges are dates
quiz.explain: With an exclusive upper bound the first range ends just before 12:00, so the ranges are adjacent, not overlapping.

concepts.name: Full-text search
concepts.summary: Search natural-language text with tsvector, tsquery, ranking and a GIN index, without a separate search engine.
concepts.why: Built-in full-text search covers many product search needs without running a separate search system.
concepts.body:
`LIKE` matches characters; **full-text search** matches *words*. It knows that 'running' and 'run' are the same word (**stemming**), skips filler words like 'the' (**stop words**), and ranks results by how well they match.

- A **tsvector** is a document reduced to base-form words (**lexemes**) with their positions: `to_tsvector('english', 'The cats are running')` gives `'cat':2 'run':4`.
- A **tsquery** is a search condition: `to_tsquery('english', 'cat & run')`. For text people type into a search box, use `websearch_to_tsquery`: it understands `"quoted phrases"`, `or` and `-excluded` words, and never fails on odd input.
- `@@` tests a match; `ts_rank` or `ts_rank_cd` scores it; `ts_headline` builds a snippet with the matching words highlighted.

For speed, store the tsvector in a **generated column** (one PostgreSQL computes from the other columns whenever a row is written) and index it with GIN, so it isn't recomputed for every row at query time. `setweight` lets title matches rank above body matches.

The text search configuration (`english`, `simple`, `russian`...) decides how text is split into words, how they're stemmed and which are stop words; use the same one for documents and queries. `simple` does no stemming, so it works for any language and for names and codes.

Limits: no tolerance for typos (combine with `pg_trgm` similarity), basic relevance tuning, and no per-category counts (facets) like a shop's filter sidebar. When you need those at scale, a dedicated search engine fed from PostgreSQL is the next step.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE article (
    id    int PRIMARY KEY,
    title text NOT NULL,
    body  text NOT NULL,
    tsv   tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
            setweight(to_tsvector('english', title), 'A') ||
            setweight(to_tsvector('english', body), 'B')) STORED
);
CREATE INDEX article_tsv_idx ON article USING gin (tsv);
INSERT INTO article (id, title, body) VALUES
 (1, 'Running PostgreSQL in production', 'Backups, monitoring and tuning.'),
 (2, 'A guide to indexes', 'Why the database runs faster with the right index.');

SELECT id, title, ts_rank(tsv, q) AS rank
FROM article, websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'run index') AS q
WHERE tsv @@ q ORDER BY rank DESC;
-- 2 | A guide to indexes | ...   ('runs' and 'index' both match)

SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The cats are running');   -- 'cat':2 'run':4
takeaways: tsvector = processed document, tsquery = search condition, @@ = match
Store the tsvector in a generated column with a GIN index
websearch_to_tsquery safely parses user-typed searches
pitfalls: Using different text search configurations for the document and the query, so stems don't match.

quiz.q: Why does to_tsvector('english', 'running') match to_tsquery('english', 'runs')?
options: Both are stemmed to the lexeme 'run'
quiz.explain: The English configuration stems both words to 'run', so the lexemes are equal.

concepts.name: Triggers and LISTEN/NOTIFY
concepts.summary: Run PL/pgSQL on row changes with BEFORE and AFTER triggers, and notify listeners with NOTIFY.
concepts.why: Triggers enforce rules and maintain derived data for every writer; NOTIFY pushes changes to apps.
concepts.body:
A **trigger** runs a function automatically when rows are inserted, updated, deleted or truncated. The function is written as `RETURNS trigger` and sees the special variables `NEW` and `OLD` (the row after and before), `TG_OP` (`'INSERT'`, `'UPDATE'`...), and `TG_TABLE_NAME`.

- **BEFORE ROW** triggers can modify `NEW` before it is written (set `updated_at`, normalise values) or skip the row by returning `NULL`.
- **AFTER ROW** triggers see the final row and are used for audit logs (a permanent record of who changed what), maintaining counters or summary tables, and notifications.
- **Statement-level** triggers (`FOR EACH STATEMENT`) run once per statement; with transition tables (`REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS ...`) they can process all changed rows in one set-based step, which is much faster for bulk changes.
- `WHEN (OLD.status IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.status)` limits when a trigger fires.

Triggers run inside the same transaction, so they're consistent — and their cost is added to every write. Keep them small, avoid long chains of triggers firing triggers, and document them: hidden behaviour surprises developers.

**LISTEN/NOTIFY** is a lightweight message channel: `NOTIFY channel, 'payload'` (or `pg_notify()`) inside a trigger delivers a message to every session that ran `LISTEN channel`, but only when the transaction commits. It's good for telling apps to throw away data they have cached. It is not a reliable queue: listeners that aren't connected at that moment miss the message.
takeaways: BEFORE ROW triggers can change NEW; AFTER triggers react to final rows
Statement triggers with transition tables are efficient for bulk changes
NOTIFY is delivered on commit and isn't durable
pitfalls: Putting slow work (calls to other web services, heavy queries) in triggers and slowing every write.

quiz.q: A BEFORE INSERT row trigger function returns NULL. What happens?
options: The row is inserted with all NULLs
The insert of that row is silently skipped
quiz.explain: Returning NULL from a BEFORE row trigger skips the operation for that row.

concepts.name: VACUUM and autovacuum
concepts.summary: Why dead tuples accumulate, how autovacuum cleans them, and how to tune it and spot bloat and wraparound risk.
concepts.why: Neglected vacuum is behind most PostgreSQL bloat, slowdowns and the dreaded transaction ID wraparound.
concepts.body:
Because of MVCC, an `UPDATE` writes a new row version and a `DELETE` only marks the old one dead. **VACUUM** reclaims the space of dead row versions that no running transaction can still see, so new rows can reuse it; it doesn't normally make the file smaller. It also updates the **visibility map** (a per-table note of which pages hold only rows everyone can see, which lets queries answer from an index alone) and **freezes** old rows.

Freezing matters. Each transaction gets an ID from a 32-bit counter, about 4 billion values, which eventually wraps round to the start. Before an old row's ID gets too far behind, VACUUM must mark the row as frozen, meaning 'older than everything'. Otherwise PostgreSQL will eventually refuse writes to protect the data. Autovacuum runs these anti-wraparound vacuums automatically; your job is not to block them.

**Autovacuum** is the background helper that starts cleanup workers for a table once its dead rows exceed `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor * reltuples` (reltuples is the table's row count; the defaults are 50 + 20%). For large tables 20% is far too late, so lower the scale factor per table: `ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01)`. Autovacuum also runs `ANALYZE` to refresh statistics.

What stops vacuum from cleaning: long-running transactions, sessions left idle inside a transaction, abandoned replication slots, and prepared transactions (two-phase commits never finished). Each holds back the **xmin horizon**, the oldest transaction whose view of the data must be kept. Watch `pg_stat_user_tables` (`n_dead_tup`, `last_autovacuum`) and `pg_stat_activity`.

`VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table to give space back to the operating system, but locks the table completely the whole time; tools like `pg_repack` do the same while the table stays in use.
takeaways: UPDATE and DELETE leave dead tuples that VACUUM makes reusable
Lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor for large tables
Long transactions and stale replication slots block cleanup
pitfalls: Disabling autovacuum to 'save resources' and later facing bloat or wraparound shutdown.

quiz.q: Autovacuum is running but dead tuples keep growing on all tables. What's a likely cause?
options: A long-running or idle-in-transaction session holding back the xmin horizon
quiz.explain: VACUUM can only remove versions no transaction can see; an old open transaction pins them.

concepts.name: Locks, blocking and job queues
concepts.summary: Find who blocks whom with pg_stat_activity and pg_blocking_pids, and build job queues with SKIP LOCKED.
concepts.why: When the app hangs, the cause is usually a lock chain you can find in a minute with the right query.
concepts.body:
Every statement takes locks. Ordinary reads and writes take weak table locks that don't conflict with each other, plus row locks for modified rows. Schema changes take `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, which conflicts with everything — including plain `SELECT`.

Lock waits **queue**: if `ALTER TABLE` waits behind a long transaction, every new query on that table then waits behind the `ALTER TABLE`. That's how a "quick migration" takes down an application. Defence: `SET lock_timeout = '3s'` before DDL, so it gives up quickly instead of blocking everyone, and try again later.

To diagnose a hang:

- `pg_stat_activity` shows every session, identified by `pid` (the id of the server process serving it): `state` (`active`, `idle in transaction`), `wait_event_type` (`Lock` means waiting on a lock), `xact_start` and the current `query`.
- `pg_blocking_pids(pid)` returns the sessions blocking a given one.
- `pg_locks` has the raw lock table.
- `pg_cancel_backend(pid)` cancels a query; `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` ends the session.

Row-level locking clauses: `FOR UPDATE` (will modify), `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` (weaker, used by ordinary updates), `FOR SHARE`. Add `NOWAIT` to fail immediately, or **`SKIP LOCKED`** to skip rows other sessions hold. `SKIP LOCKED` turns a table into a reliable job queue: each worker (one of several copies of your background program) claims different rows without waiting for the others.

Set `log_lock_waits = on` so waits longer than `deadlock_timeout` are logged.
takeaways: Lock waits queue: DDL behind a long transaction blocks everyone after it
pg_stat_activity + pg_blocking_pids find the blocker
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED builds safe concurrent job queues
pitfalls: Terminating the blocked session instead of the one holding the lock.

quiz.q: Several workers run SELECT ... LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a job table at once. What happens?
options: They all get the same row and wait
All but one get an error
Each gets a different unlocked row without waiting
quiz.explain: SKIP LOCKED ignores rows locked by others, so each worker claims a different job.

concepts.name: Declarative partitioning in practice
concepts.summary: Partition large tables by range, attach and detach partitions concurrently, and keep pruning working.
concepts.why: Partitioning makes deleting old data instant and keeps huge tables of events over time manageable, if you avoid its traps.
concepts.body:
`PARTITION BY RANGE | LIST | HASH` turns a table into a parent with no storage of its own; rows are routed to child partitions. Practical points beyond the basics:

- **Create partitions ahead of time** (with a scheduled job or the `pg_partman` extension). Inserts with no matching partition fail, unless you add a `DEFAULT` partition — which then must be scanned when new partitions are attached, so keep it empty.
- **Indexes** created on the parent are created on every partition automatically. A primary key or unique constraint must **include the partition key**, because uniqueness is only enforced within each partition.
- **Retention**: `ALTER TABLE ... DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY` then `DROP TABLE` removes a month of data instantly, leaving no bloat (wasted space from deleted rows) behind, far better than a mass `DELETE`.
- **Loading**: build and index a table separately, add a matching `CHECK` constraint, then `ATTACH PARTITION`; the check lets PostgreSQL skip validating the rows.
- **Pruning** happens while planning for values written in the query, and while running for values passed in separately; it only works when the `WHERE` clause constrains the partition key directly.

Don't over-partition: thousands of partitions slow planning and use more memory. Partitions of a few GB to tens of GB are typical. Partitioning helps maintenance and pruning; it doesn't make single-row lookups by an indexed key faster.
takeaways: Create partitions in advance; keep any DEFAULT partition empty
Unique keys must include the partition key
DETACH ... CONCURRENTLY + DROP is instant, bloat-free retention
pitfalls: Querying by a function of the partition key (date(created_at) = ...), which defeats pruning.

quiz.q: Why must the primary key of a partitioned table include the partition key?
options: PostgreSQL requires every column in the key
Uniqueness is enforced only within each partition's own index
quiz.explain: There is no global index, so only a key containing the partition key is guaranteed unique overall.

concepts.name: Row-level security
concepts.summary: Restrict which rows each role or customer can see and change, with policies the database enforces on every query.
concepts.why: When many customers share the same tables, RLS keeps each one's rows apart even if application code forgets a WHERE clause.
concepts.body:
**Row-level security** (RLS) adds per-row filters enforced by PostgreSQL itself. Enable it on a table with `ALTER TABLE t ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`; from then on, roles subject to it see **no rows** until a policy allows them.

A **policy** has:

- a command (`FOR SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `ALL`),
- target roles (`TO app`),
- `USING (expr)`: which existing rows are visible or can be updated/deleted,
- `WITH CHECK (expr)`: which new or modified rows are allowed to be written.

Policies are combined with OR (permissive, the default) or AND (`AS RESTRICTIVE`).

A common pattern when many customers (tenants) share tables: for each request it handles, the application sets a custom setting, `SET app.tenant_id = '42'` (or `set_config('app.tenant_id', '42', true)` inside the transaction), and the policy compares `tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int`. When connections are reused through a connection pool, use the transaction-local form so a value can't leak to the next request.

Important exemptions: **superusers** and roles with `BYPASSRLS` ignore RLS, and so does the **table owner** unless you add `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. So the application must not connect as the owner. Index the columns used in policies; the policy's condition is added to every query, so keep it, and any functions it calls, simple.
takeaways: ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY + policies filter rows for every query
USING filters visible rows; WITH CHECK checks rows being written
Owners and superusers bypass RLS unless FORCE is set
pitfalls: Testing RLS as the table owner or a superuser and concluding it works (or doesn't).

quiz.q: RLS is enabled with a USING policy, but the app still sees every tenant's rows. What's the most likely cause?
options: The app connects as the table owner or a superuser
The policy has no WITH CHECK
quiz.explain: Owners (without FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY) and superusers are exempt from policies.

concepts.name: Extensions and pg_stat_statements
concepts.summary: Install extensions with CREATE EXTENSION and find your most expensive queries with pg_stat_statements.
concepts.why: pg_stat_statements is the first tool to reach for in performance work, and extensions are PostgreSQL's superpower.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL is built to be extended: new types, functions, operators, index types and background programs can be packaged as **extensions**. `CREATE EXTENSION name` installs one into the current database (its files must already be on the server); `\dx` lists installed ones. Managed services allow a chosen list. Update one with `ALTER EXTENSION name UPDATE`.

Well-known extensions that ship with PostgreSQL: **pg_stat_statements** (query statistics), **pg_trgm**, **btree_gist**, **pgcrypto** (encryption functions) and **postgres_fdw** (query tables on another server).

Popular ones you install separately: **PostGIS** (maps and geometry), **pgvector** (finds the closest matches among embeddings: lists of numbers that represent meaning), **pg_cron** (scheduled jobs), **pg_partman** (splitting big tables into parts by date), **TimescaleDB** (data recorded over time) and **Citus** (spreading tables across several servers).

**pg_stat_statements** groups statements that differ only in their values (it shows `$1` in place of each constant) and keeps running totals for each: number of calls, total and average time, rows, and pages read. It must be listed in `shared_preload_libraries`, the setting for add-ons loaded at server start (so it needs a restart), and then created with `CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements`.

The most useful query sorts by `total_exec_time`: the statements that use the most server time overall. That is often a fast query called millions of times rather than the slowest single one.
